content: Vision loss can occur due to various causes, including opacities in the eye's media, retinal diseases, optic nerve disorders, visual pathway abnormalities, functional disorders, or central nervous system abnormalities. The classification of vision loss is essential for understanding its pathophysiology and guiding treatment. Vision loss can be unilateral or bilateral, transient or persistent, sudden or gradual, painless or painful. Media Opacity Opacities in the eye's clear refractive media, such as the cornea, anterior chamber, lens, or vitreous humor, can lead to acute visual loss. This is often characterized by blurry vision or reduced visual acuity. While pupillary reflexes may be affected, these conditions typically do not cause a relative afferent pupillary defect. Common causes include corneal edema, hyphema, cataracts, and vitreous hemorrhage. Retinal Disease Retinal diseases can result in sudden visual loss. Since the retina is involved, a relative afferent pupillary defect is often present. Examples include macular degeneration and retinal vascular occlusions, with central retinal artery occlusion being particularly significant. Optic Nerve Disease Diseases affecting the optic nerve can cause acute visual loss. Signs include an abnormal pupillary reflex, with a relative afferent pupillary defect in unilateral cases. Conditions affecting the optic nerve include optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis, papillitis, papilledema, glaucoma, ischemic optic neuropathy, and giant cell arteritis. Hypoxia The eye is highly sensitive to oxygen deprivation. Vision dimming, described as a brownout or grayout, along with peripheral vision loss, can occur due to low blood pressure, shock, G-LOC (gravity-induced loss of consciousness in aviation), or sudden postural changes, especially in individuals who are ill or debilitated. Vision typically recovers once blood flow is restored. Visual Pathway Disorders Disorders of the visual pathway can impede visual processing. Rarely, acute visual loss may result from homonymous hemianopia or, even more rarely, cortical blindness. Functional Disorders The term functional disorder has replaced older terms like hysterical or malingering to acknowledge the physician's inability to fully assess the subjective visual experience of a patient. Causes of Vision Loss Transient Vision Loss (<24 hours) Amaurosis fugax: Unilateral vision loss lasting minutes. Migraine: Vision loss lasting 10–60 minutes. Ocular ischemic syndrome (carotid occlusive disease). Papilledema: Raised intracranial pressure. Malignant hypertension. Retinal detachment. Orthostatic hypotension: Sudden blood pressure changes. Acute angle-closure glaucoma. Vitreous hemorrhage or detachment. Vertebrobasilar artery insufficiency: Bilateral vision loss lasting minutes. Vision Loss >24 hours: Sudden, Painless Exposure to intense light (e.g., welder's flash). Ischemic optic neuropathy: Rule out giant cell arteritis. Retinal or CNS diseases: Occipital lobe CVA causing cortical blindness. Optic neuritis. Retinal artery/vein occlusion. Retinal detachment. Vitreous or aqueous hemorrhage (e.g., hyphema). Vision Loss >24 hours: Gradual, Painless Cataracts. Cerebral neoplasm. Chronic retinopathy: Diabetic or age-related macular degeneration. Chronic corneal disease: Corneal dystrophy or ulcer. Open-angle glaucoma. Optic neuropathy/atrophy. Toxic-metabolic causes. Refractive error. Retinitis pigmentosa. Vision Loss >24 hours: Painful Acute angle-closure glaucoma. Corneal hydrops: Keratoconus or corneal abrasion/ulcer. Herpes simplex/zoster. Uveitis. Optic neuritis. Orbital apex syndrome. Life-Threatening Causes Certain conditions, such as giant cell arteritis, require immediate attention to prevent permanent vision loss or systemic complications. Diagnosis History and Symptoms Key elements include: Age and onset of vision loss. Rate of progression. History of trauma or headaches. Medication and medical history. Alcohol, drug, or tobacco use. Physical Examination Focus on: Visual acuity. Blood pressure. Color vision. Cranial nerve function. Fundus examination. Intraocular pressure. Ocular media clarity. Optic disc evaluation. Laboratory Findings Tests may include: ESR, fasting blood glucose, HbA1c. PPD, RPR, FTA-ABS. ACE levels, vitamin B12, and folate. Imaging CT or MRI of the head and chest may be necessary for further evaluation. Treatment Medical Therapy Systemic steroids: For temporal arteritis, optic neuritis, pituitary apoplexy, herpes zoster, or non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. Aspirin: For cavernous sinus thrombosis. Antibiotics or anticoagulation: As indicated. Cycloplegic agents or hypertonic NaCl ointment: For corneal hydrops. Surgical Interventions Corneal transplant: For corneal hydrops. Surgical repair: For retinal detachment. Cataract removal: For advanced cataracts. Temporal artery biopsy and steroids: For temporal arteritis.
